words.understanding:
The posterior strongly favors a weakening of the right‑side actuators (≈90 % weight, factor ≈0.17), with a smaller chance of left‑side weakness (≈10 %). Sensor bias has negligible support. The current behavior—almost no steps, small forward pitch, negative capture margin—is consistent with weakened actuation on one side causing instability.

Uncertainty remains whether the deficit is on the right or left leg (the two leading hypotheses split the remaining probability). Distinguishing this will tell us which side to strengthen and avoid wasted effort on the wrong side.
words.uncertainty: We need to discriminate between actuator_strength:right and actuator_strength:left explanations. The sensor_bias:pitch hypothesis is already implausible, but an experiment that yields different walking outcomes for the two actuator hypotheses will sharply reduce entropy and pinpoint the affected side.
words.why: Running a frequency reduction (cf:freq@x0.85) yields starkly different predictions: under right‑side weakness the robot is expected to walk in nearly all trials (≈4/4 steps), whereas under left‑side weakness it is expected to fail almost completely (≈0/4 steps). This contrast will quickly resolve the left/right ambiguity, guiding a targeted repair (e.g., boosting right actuator strength) and is more informative than the engine’s default suggestion.

words.understanding: The posterior overwhelmingly points to a weakening of the right‑side actuators (factor ≈0.17). This loss of torque reduces push‑off, leading to very short steps, low forward velocity, high double‑support time and a negative capture margin – the robot barely stays upright. Lowering the gait frequency partially alleviates the asymmetry, showing that timing adjustments can help compensate.
words.uncertainty: We do not know the precise magnitude of the right‑actuator deficit, whether other minor deviations (e.g., left‑side weakness, sensor bias, friction changes) are present, and which repair subsystem (feedback gains, posture bias, timing, etc.) will most effectively counteract the weakness without causing new instabilities.
words.why: Screening the repair tools under the current belief costs no plant rollouts and will identify the most promising tool (e.g., feedback or posture) to address right‑actuator weakness. This zero‑cost information focuses any subsequent plant‑budgeted repair attempt, increasing the chance of success while conserving limited resources for validation.

words.understanding: The posterior is almost entirely concentrated on a weakening of the right‑side actuators (factor ≈0.17). This accounts for the observed lack of steps, low forward speed, negative capture margin and the improvement when gait frequency is lowered. However, the freq@x0.85 test shows a systematic residual in double_support_fraction (‑1.1 noise units), indicating that the actuator‑weakness‑only model mispredicts stance timing. This suggests that additional mechanical or sensory changes (e.g., altered joint damping, sensor bias, or foot friction) may be present.
words.uncertainty: We do not yet know whether the deficit is solely due to reduced right‑side torque or whether it is accompanied by changes such as increased joint damping on the right, a pitch sensor bias, reduced foot‑floor friction, or a weakening of the left‑side actuators. These alternatives could explain the timing residual and would affect which repair tools are most effective.
words.why: Adding alternative hypotheses will diversify the belief, giving future experiments non‑zero expected information gain and allowing us to discriminate between pure actuator weakness and combined causes before committing to a repair.

The only notable unexplained residual is the double‑support fraction when frequency is reduced, suggesting that timing or geometric parameters may also be off, but the actuator hypothesis remains dominant.
words.uncertainty: Whether the observed frequency‑dependent residual stems from a secondary issue such as joint damping, sensor bias, or a leg‑length mismatch that would require a different repair tool (e.g., leg_length or timing) is still unclear.
words.why: The engine’s delegate_repair procedure will automatically screen repair tools under the current belief, run a robust simulator optimisation on the top‑ranked tool (leg_length), and then perform a budget‑aware plant‑based CMA‑ES search, making the most efficient use of the remaining 692 plant rollouts and 1176 simulation budget to converge on a repair that addresses the identified actuator weakness while also exploring possible secondary causes.

words.understanding: The posterior concentrates on a unilateral loss of actuator strength, with ~90% probability on the right side and ~10% on the left. Both explain the observed zero walking, short upright time (~10 s) and near‑zero pitch mean, but they remain indistinguishable. The key uncertainty is which side (or both) is actually weakened, as this determines the appropriate repair (strengthening the deficient side).
words.uncertainty: Whether the dominant defect lies in the right actuator, the left actuator, or a symmetric weakness that the current two‑hypothesis split cannot resolve.
words.why: Experiment cf:freq@x0.85 has high expected information gain (0.34 nats) and yields divergent walk predictions: under a right‑side weakness it predicts walking in both trials, under a left‑side weakness predicts none, allowing discrimination between the leading explanations at low plant cost (4 rollouts).

words.understanding: The posterior strongly favors a unilateral loss of actuator strength on the right side (factor≈0.17). This explains the lack of walking and low forward speed, but the model fails to predict the change in double_support_fraction when the gait frequency is reduced (residual –1.1 noise units). This suggests the current deviation does not capture all relevant physics—perhaps the left side is also weakened, joint damping is altered, or a sensor bias affects pitch estimation. We have not yet tested left‑side actuator strength, asymmetric damping, or pitch sensor bias.
words.uncertainty: Which side(s) of the actuator are weakened, whether joint damping (especially on the left) is increased, and if a constant pitch sensor bias is present. These uncertainties affect which repair tools (e.g., placement vs posture vs feedback) will be effective.
words.why: Adding explicit hypotheses for left‑side actuator strength, left‑side joint damping, and a pitch sensor bias will give the belief engine distinct alternatives to weigh against the current right‑only actuator explanation. Future experiments (e.g., frequency tweaks, stance‑knee changes) will then produce discriminative residuals, allowing the engine to update weights and focus the subsequent repair search on the true cause.

words.understanding: The belief engine has converged on a unilateral loss of actuator strength on the right side (factor ≈ 0.17) as the dominant explanation, accounting for the robot's inability to walk, low forward speed, and near‑zero pitch. The only notable mismatch is the under‑prediction of double_support_fraction when the gait frequency is lowered, suggesting the current deviation may not fully capture timing‑related effects, but the posterior weight on alternative mechanisms (sensor bias, joint damping, left‑side weakness, etc.) remains negligible.
words.uncertainty: We are not yet certain whether the right‑side actuator weakness alone is sufficient or whether a secondary timing or joint‑damping deviation contributes to the observed double_support_fraction residual. Until we gather discriminative data, the exact nature of the deviation stays ambiguous.
words.why: Given the strong posterior on a clear mechanical deficit (right actuator strength) and the limited plant budget remaining, the engine’s automated repair procedure is the most efficient path forward. It will first screen repair tools under the current belief, then perform a simulator‑based optimisation of the top tool, followed by a real‑robot CMA‑ES search that allocates the remaining budget to the most promising tools and stops early if a passing design is found. This approach maximises the chance of recovering walking while conserving plant rollouts for final verification.
